extracted.intended_audience: practicing patent attorneys, law students, and judges (U.S. patent litigation practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary rules for equitable defenses (laches, equitable estoppel), injunctive relief, stays, and monetary damages in U.S. patent litigation, including how to prove lost profits and royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches defense — elements and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patent owner “dealt unfairly with the alleged infringer by not promptly bringing suit.” The alleged infringer bears the burden of proving the laches elements by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the delay exceeded six years, the elements are presumed and the patent owner has a burden of going forward with evidence to “burst” the presumption by showing a reasonable excuse for the delay or that the delay did not cause injury. Laches requires a balancing of equities and can be defeated by egregious conduct of the alleged infringer related to laches facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches — commencement and responsibility for delay
rubrics_metrics.description: The period of delay begins when the patent owner knows, or in the exercise of reasonable diligence should have known, of the alleged infringer’s acts. The patent owner asserting the patent is responsible for delays of any previous owners of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable diligence standard; a patent owner can be charged with prior owners’ delay when asserting the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches — reasonable excuses and unreasonable excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of reasonable excuses for delay include: the patent owner was suing a different party for infringement of the same patent; the patent owner was negotiating a license with the alleged infringer; and a war was being waged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally unreasonable excuses include that the patent owner was too poor, too sick, or that the alleged infringer was not worth suing because he or she was too poor. The equities may require the patent owner to inform the alleged infringer of its reasons for delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches — prejudice types and remedial effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudice to the alleged infringer resulting from the patent owner’s delay can be evidentiary (loss of records, death of a witness, unreliable memories) or economic (loss of investments, damages preventable by an earlier suit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If laches is established, the patent owner is precluded from recovering for all infringement that occurred before the complaint was filed; however, laches does not necessarily bar injunctions or recovery of post-filing damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable estoppel — three-element test
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable estoppel focuses on what the alleged infringer was led to reasonably believe by the patent owner’s conduct. The usual defense requires: (1) misleading conduct by the patent owner leading the alleged infringer reasonably to infer non-enforcement; (2) reliance by the alleged infringer (a relationship or communication that lulled the infringer into a sense of security); and (3) material prejudice to the alleged infringer because of that reliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misleading conduct may be specific statements, action, inaction, or silence where there was an obligation to speak. Material prejudice can be evidentiary or economic. The alleged infringer bears the burden by a preponderance of the evidence (absent fraud/intentional misconduct). Even if the three elements are established, courts consider other equities before barring the suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable estoppel — relation to delay presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike laches, a six-year delay does not give rise to any presumption in equitable estoppel, though delay may be relevant to whether conduct was misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit law changed estoppel analysis; caution required when relying on pre-Aukerman precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies available to successful patent owner
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies include (1) preliminary and permanent injunctions; (2) monetary damages generally corresponding to lost profits, established or reasonable royalties, and interest; (3) increased (enhanced) damages; and (4) attorney fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 284 mandates damages 'adequate to compensate' but at least a reasonable royalty; damages may be increased up to three times at the district court’s discretion; injunctive relief and monetary relief are distinct and subject to separate doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 284 damages standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages must be adequate to compensate for the infringement, but in no event less than a reasonable royalty; compensatory awards typically take the form of lost profits, established or reasonable royalties, interest, and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee is entitled to full compensation for injuries proximately caused by infringement, which may be calculated by methods other than lost profits or royalties when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction — four-factor test
rubrics_metrics.description: Four factors to decide entitlement to a preliminary injunction: (1) reasonable likelihood of success on the merits; (2) whether the movant would suffer irreparable harm absent the injunction; (3) whether the balance of hardships tips in the movant’s favor; and (4) the injunction’s impact on the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each factor must be weighed against the others and the relief sought; a district court may deny relief based on failure to establish either of the first two factors; the Federal Circuit warns that preliminary injunctions are drastic and not routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction — what constitutes likelihood of success and irreparable harm
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner will show reasonable likelihood of success by clearly showing that the patent is valid, enforceable, and infringed, though a lesser showing may suffice. A clear showing of validity and infringement raises a rebuttable presumption of irreparable harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebutting circumstances include patent owner’s delay in bringing suit, licensing of the patent, whether the patent owner practices the patent, large market share comparisons, and alleged infringer’s inability to pay money damages. The presumption is rebuttable by such circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent injunction — general rule and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: General rule: an injunction will issue when infringement has been adjudged unless there is a sound reason for denying it. If established, equitable reasons such as granting a compulsory license or finding that a damage award was essentially a life-of-patent license may justify denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumstances that are not sound reasons to deny include small infringer sales relative to patentee, that the infringer would be put out of business, or that the infringer has stopped infringing. Any injunction must be specific regarding the enjoined conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay of injunction pending appeal — four-factor test
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors considered: (1) whether the stay applicant has made a strong showing of likely success on appeal; (2) whether the stay applicant will be irreparably injured if stay not granted; (3) whether issuing a stay will substantially injure other interested parties; and (4) where the public interest lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The factors need not be equally weighted; a great harm to the applicant can lessen the required strength of showing on the merits. Relevant considerations include layoffs/insolvency for irreparable injury, effect on patentee’s ability to execute judgment and existing licenses for injury to others, and public access to infringing products for public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary damages measures — lost profits vs royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional measures under 35 U.S.C. § 284 are lost profits and royalties (established or reasonable). The lost profits measure is appropriate when the patentee and infringer compete in the same market; the royalty measure is appropriate when an established royalty exists or lost profits cannot be proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee is not limited to these measures and may recover other damages adequate to compensate for proximate injuries; in no event may damages be less than a reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — nature of recoverable losses
rubrics_metrics.description: A prevailing patentee is entitled to profits lost because of diverted sales, price erosion, and increased costs, where provable; such awards are typically composed of the patentee’s lost profits rather than infringer’s profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits must be proven as a matter of fact; recent decisions have eased the showing required to satisfy the burden of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving lost profits — Panduit test (four elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panduit test requires proof of: (1) demand for the patented product; (2) absence of acceptable noninfringing substitutes; (3) the patentee’s manufacturing and marketing capability to exploit the demand; and (4) the amount of profit the patentee would have made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit approves Panduit as the starting point but not the exclusive method. Proof of significant sales is compelling evidence of demand. The patentee need only show a reasonable probability it would have made some or all of the infringer’s sales; it need not rule out all other possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of acceptable noninfringing substitutes — evidentiary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolved requirement: show either (1) purchasers generally were willing to buy the patented product for its advantages, or (2) specific purchasers of the infringing product purchased on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Available noninfringing substitutes of significantly higher cost are not acceptable substitutes for damages calculation. Market surveys, testimony that purchasers would have bought from the patentee, or proof of a long-felt need can be probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: State Industries (market-share) method as an alternative to Panduit's second element
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee and infringer compete in the same market, the patentee may use a market-share approach (State Industries) to estimate additional sales it would have made, allowing the patentee to ignore Panduit’s second element (absence of substitutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analysis applies only when customers of the infringer would transfer demand to the patentee’s product if the infringing product were unavailable; it is permissible but not mandatory and has specific applicability limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing and marketing capability proof for lost profits
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet Panduit’s third element, the patentee must show adequate manufacturing and marketing capability to meet the additional demand; proof of ability to expand capacity suffices even if capacity did not exist during infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even limited bidding by the patentee on contracts that cover only a small portion of the infringer’s sales does not preclude recovery of lost profits on all infringing sales if capability to meet demand is established.
